What is this material made of that electrons can't shoot through without slits?

It doesn't need to be non-conductive. Color CRT screens had electrons whizzing through a metal mask perforated with tiny holes. The mask would develop a charge but it was negligible to the fast moving electrons and they would hit the phosphor coating just fine. The charge on the material used would have to be very high in order to deflect the electron significantly at the speed they are moving.

https://www.quora.com/What-kind-of-materials-have-been-used-for-double-slit-experiments

Do you mean for the slits? Metals, various glasses, silicone wafers, even “intense beams of light” when looking for diffraction in large molecules.

The material can be anything, including metal. Old color CRTs used a perforated metal mask to direct and focus the electron beams to the phosphor coating on the front of the tube. The holes in the mask (or screen if you prefer) were quite small but larger than the gap in the double slit experiment. That really doesn't matter much since the gap is what is important. So long as the material of the slit mask is not overly charged positive or negative, the electrons will happily go whizzing by since they are moving at near relativistic speeds (for the medium they travel in at least). You would need a strong like or opposite charge on the slit material in order to deflect these fast moving electrons. CRTs had to use significant high voltages and magnetic fields to steer the electron beams so a very weak charge of field would be negligible to their path.

While I have seen Young's double slit experiment done with an electron beam and a phosphor screen to render the interference pattern, most setups use light so the slits can definitely be made of anything at all. Way back in my high school Physics class we did the experiment as a lab. We painted microscope slides with a graphite paint and let it dry. We then took two safety razor blades and stacked them to a double thickness. The blade edges were separated by about one-half the thickness of the metal in one blade. We scored the graphite coating on the slide with this razor blade arrangement and got two very closely spaced and narrow slits. This allowed us to take a reference light source at a known distance from the slits and a paper target and observe the interference pattern it made. It was astounding to see it then and more so now to remember that I was observing a quantum phenomenon of significant importance though our lab experiment hardly scratched the surface of the topic. It was the best day for me in my old Physics class.
